doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago pianists, Tatum and talent versus practice
title: Playing piano first; Prentice McCarey on 55th Street
summary: Freeman talks of his piano facility, marriage reception at a 55th Street club and pianist Prentice McCarey.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: So you started playing piano before you started playing saxophone. You were proficient on piano before saxophone?
Sure, I could run up and down everything. They used to call me Runs. I was a great admirer of Art Tatum
Who wasn’t? Art Tatum was the man.

You know something? I was playing a club on 55th Street. This club was a famous club, because Coleman Hawkins used to come there, back in his heyday. I got married. My reception was in this club where I was working, this famous club, right down from the Rhumboogie, going west.

There was an elevated on 55th, elevated station, and I was right to the west of this elevated station at a place – I’m trying – this place had three or four big-time names. All the big-time horn players used to come to this place. It was upstairs, a gorgeous room. You had to go up some long stairs. I remember distinctly Coleman Hawkins playing there. I think Fletcher Henderson’s band played there. I used to practice all the time, like 20 hours a day. I was living over this great piano player. I didn’t know he was this great. His name was Prentice McCarey.

Prentice. So I’d be banging on this piano. Oh, I’d go nuts. My mother loved it. So she said, “Play, boy, play.” She’d be sitting on a chair. I’m just playing. Then finally I started playing the saxophone. He used to call up and say, “Please. Piano, maybe.” “But,” he said, “saxophone.” He said, “I can’t stand it. Stop.” The funny part about it was, years later, I got to play in this place myself, and guess who I hired?

Prentice McCarey, one of my idols. He’s a great piano player. Every time Coleman Hawkins came to town, he would use this cat. He never practiced. He was the first guy to tell me – he said, “I don’t practice any more physically. I practice mentally.” Just like I practice today now. He said, “Once I get it up here, I got it.” I used to say, “Really?” He said, “Yeah, you’ll reach it, maybe 50 years from now.” That’s what he used to tell me. And sure enough, I did.
He was older than you then.
